Clinical Reference · Hematology

Anemia — Diagnostic Workup & Management

On this page
Anemia is a reduction in red-cell mass (WHO: hemoglobin <13 g/dL in men, <12 g/dL in non-pregnant women, <11 in pregnancy). It is a sign, never a final diagnosis — the whole job of the workup is to find the mechanism. Two axes do the triage: the reticulocyte response (is the marrow making cells?) crossed with the MCV (how big are the cells?).
WHO cutoff ♂ <13 · ♀ <12 g/dL MCV: <80 micro · 80–100 normo · >100 macro RPI <2 = under-production Ferritin <30 ng/mL = iron deficiency Transfuse at Hgb 7 g/dL (restrictive, AABB 2023)
Shared

Pathophysiology & the diagnostic logic

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Red cells are made in the marrow under drive from erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone released by peritubular fibroblasts in the kidney when they sense low oxygen delivery. Each red cell needs three raw materials to mature: iron (for heme), and vitamin B12 + folate (for the DNA of the dividing precursor). A finished cell survives ~120 days, then is recycled by splenic macrophages — which hand the iron back for reuse. Anemia appears when any part of this fails, and there are only three ways it can fail:

  • Under-production (hypoproliferative) — the factory is slow: missing raw material (iron, B12, folate), missing signal (no EPO in CKD), a suppressed or crowded marrow (inflammation, malignancy, aplasia), or a broken assembly line (MDS). The reticulocyte count is low.
  • Destruction (hemolysis) — cells are made fine but shredded early: antibody-coated (autoimmune), fragmented by fibrin or valves (microangiopathy), or intrinsically fragile (membrane, enzyme, or hemoglobin defects). The marrow revs up, so reticulocytes are high.
  • Loss (bleeding) — cells leave the body: GI, GYN, trauma, surgery. Reticulocytes rise after a few days; ongoing loss also drains iron and eventually converts a normocytic picture into a microcytic one.
Think of red cells as a delivery fleet hauling oxygen. Anemia is either the factory building too few trucks (hypoproliferative — low reticulocytes), trucks being wrecked on the road (hemolysis — high reticulocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin), or cargo bleeding out the back (blood loss). The MCV is the size of the truck — tiny trucks (microcytic) mean the heme paint ran out (iron); oversized trucks (macrocytic) mean the DNA blueprints were incomplete (B12/folate). The reticulocyte count tells you whether the factory is even trying.
Figure 1 — The two-axis anemia algorithm: reticulocyte response first (production vs loss/destruction), then MCV to narrow the under-production causes. This is the spine of the entire workup.

Iron, hepcidin & why inflammation causes anemia

Iron is never free in the body — it is escorted. Dietary iron is absorbed in the duodenum, exported into blood by the channel ferroportin, and carried by transferrin to the marrow. The master switch is hepcidin, a liver peptide: when hepcidin is high it binds and destroys ferroportin, locking iron inside gut cells and macrophages. Inflammation (via IL-6) drives hepcidin up — so in any inflammatory state (infection, cancer, CKD, heart failure, autoimmune disease) iron is trapped, not absent. This is the mechanism of anemia of inflammation / chronic disease, and it explains two clinical facts: (1) ferritin (an iron-storage and acute-phase protein) is normal or high even when usable iron is low, and (2) oral iron often fails in inflammation because hepcidin blocks its absorption — so IV iron, which bypasses the gut, is preferred.

Figure 2 — The iron cycle and the hepcidin brake. Inflammation → IL-6 → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin degraded → iron trapped → low serum iron with high ferritin.
Erythropoiesis: the hematopoietic stem cell matures through erythroid precursors to the reticulocyte and finally the anucleate red cell. Iron feeds heme; B12/folate feed the dividing nucleus.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Hematopoiesis (human) diagram.png · A. Rad · CC BY-SA 3.0
Normal peripheral blood film for comparison — uniform biconcave red cells with central pallor no larger than a small lymphocyte nucleus.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Lymphocyte2.jpg · No machine-readable author provided. NicolasGrandjean assumed (based on copyright claims). · CC BY-SA 3.0
Every therapy in this guide maps to one broken step above: oral/IV iron refills the heme raw material; B12/folate restore DNA synthesis; ESAs (epoetin/darbepoetin) replace the missing EPO signal in CKD; transfusion is instant fleet replacement for dangerous loss; and treating the inflammation/cause lowers hepcidin so the body's own iron is freed. Keep asking: which step is broken, and which lever fixes that step?

MCV is an average. A patient with both iron deficiency (small) and B12 deficiency (large) can have a normal MCV with a high RDW — always read the RDW and glance at the smear rather than trusting the MCV alone.
⚙️

By marrow response (kinetic) — the reticulocyte axis

The reticulocyte count answers "is the marrow responding?" but must be corrected for the degree of anemia, because a percentage is misleading when the total red-cell mass is low. Correct it, then compute the Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI):

StepFormulaInterpretation
Corrected retic %retic % × (patient Hct ÷ 45)Adjusts the percent for anemia severity
RPIcorrected retic % ÷ maturation factorRPI < 2 → hypoproliferative (under-production). RPI ≥ 2–3 → appropriate marrow response = blood loss or hemolysis
Maturation factor
(by Hct)		Hct 36–45 → 1.0 · 26–35 → 1.5 · 16–25 → 2.0 · ≤15 → 2.5Reticulocytes released early ("shift cells") live longer in blood as anemia worsens, so you divide by a larger factor

Interpreting the labs — what moves, and why

🧪

Iron studies — the four numbers & their patterns

StateFerritinSerum ironTIBC / transferrinTSat
Iron deficiency↓ (<30 diagnostic; <15 classic)↓↑ (body upregulates the carrier)↓ <20%
Anemia of inflammation / chronic diseasenormal or ↑ (often >100)↓↓ or normal↓ or normal
Combined IDA + inflammation<100 (use higher cutoff)↓variable↓
Thalassemia traitnormal / ↑normal / ↑normalnormal / ↑
Sideroblastic↑↑normal / ↓↑
Iron overload (hemochromatosis)↑↑↑↓↑↑ (>45%)

Why each number moves (and the traps)

  • Ferritin reflects total iron stores and is an acute-phase reactant — infection, inflammation, liver disease, and malignancy falsely raise it. A ferritin <30 ng/mL is highly specific for iron deficiency (~98%); the AGA 2020 guideline endorses a more sensitive cutoff of <45 ng/mL in anemic patients (classic cutoffs were <15). In inflammatory states (CKD, HF, IBD, active infection) raise the bar: treat ferritin <100, or <300 with TSat <20%, as functional iron deficiency.
  • TIBC/transferrin rises in iron deficiency (the body makes more carrier to scavenge iron) but falls in inflammation and malnutrition — which is how it helps separate IDA from anemia of chronic disease.
  • Transferrin saturation (TSat = iron ÷ TIBC) <20% supports iron deficiency; very high (>45%) flags iron overload. Fasting morning samples are best (serum iron has diurnal swing and rises after iron-rich meals/supplements).
  • Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) rises in true iron deficiency but is not an acute-phase reactant — useful to unmask IDA hiding behind inflammation when ferritin is equivocal.
🧫

B12 / folate & hemolysis panels

Atrophic ("beefy-red", smooth) glossitis — a clue to B12 or iron deficiency.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Glossite.jpg · Grook Da Oger · CC BY-SA 3.0
Marrow aspirate — megaloblastic changes (large precursors, open chromatin) vs a control.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Distribution of control non-megaloblastic anemia participants & Analysis of bone marrow collected from non-megaloblastic anemia controls and megaloblastic anemia cases using Leishman’s staining.png · Yadav MK, Manoli NM, Madhunapantula SV · CC BY 4.0

B12 & folate

  • Vitamin B12 <200 pg/mL = deficient; 200–300 pg/mL is borderline → confirm with methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine: both rise in B12 deficiency; only homocysteine rises in isolated folate deficiency. MMA is the most sensitive early marker.
  • Folate <2–4 ng/mL = deficient; RBC folate reflects longer-term stores than serum folate.
  • The rule that prevents harm: never replace folate without checking/replacing B12 — giving folate alone in B12 deficiency corrects the anemia but lets the neurologic injury (subacute combined degeneration) progress irreversibly.

Hemolysis workup (send when RPI ≥ 2 without bleeding)

  • LDH ↑, indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin ↑, haptoglobin ↓, reticulocytes ↑ = the hemolysis quartet. Haptoglobin near-zero and hemoglobinuria/urine hemosiderin point to intravascular hemolysis.
  • DAT (direct antiglobulin / Coombs) splits it: positive → immune (warm IgG or cold IgM); negative → non-immune (membrane, enzyme, hemoglobinopathy, mechanical, PNH).
  • Targeted next tests: peripheral smear (schistocytes → MAHA; spherocytes → HS/warm AIHA; bite cells → G6PD), G6PD assay (check after the acute episode — young reticulocytes have higher enzyme and can mask it), hemoglobin electrophoresis (sickle, thalassemia), and flow cytometry for PNH (CD55/CD59).
Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia is a medical emergency until proven otherwise — think TTP (start plasma exchange, do not wait for ADAMTS13) or DIC. See the ICU panel.

Assess

When to suspect — presentation & why

🔍

Symptoms & signs — frequency & mechanism

Most chronic anemia is asymptomatic or vaguely fatiguing until Hgb is low or dropping fast — the body compensates with ↑cardiac output and a right-shifted O₂ curve. Symptoms track severity, acuity, and the patient's cardiopulmonary reserve.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens
Fatigue / reduced exercise tolerance~70–90%Less O₂ delivery to muscle; the most common but least specific complaint
Exertional dyspnea~50–60%Reduced O₂-carrying capacity → earlier anaerobic threshold; compensatory hyperventilation
Pallor (conjunctival, palmar crease, nail bed)~40–60%Reduced hemoglobin in the microcirculation; conjunctival rim is the most reliable exam sign
Palpitations / resting tachycardia~40–50%Compensatory ↑cardiac output to maintain O₂ delivery; a flow murmur may appear
Lightheadedness / headache~25–40%Reduced cerebral O₂ delivery; worse with orthostasis if volume-depleted
Pica / pagophagia (ice craving)~20–30% (iron def)Poorly understood but fairly specific for iron deficiency; resolves with repletion
Restless legs syndrome~15–25% (iron def)Low CNS iron alters dopaminergic signaling; check ferritin in any RLS patient
Glossitis / angular cheilitis / dysphagia~15–25%Iron/B12 needed for rapidly dividing epithelium; Plummer–Vinson = IDA + esophageal web
Koilonychia (spoon nails)<10% (chronic severe IDA)Prolonged iron deficiency softens/deforms the nail matrix
Neurologic — paresthesia, ↓proprioception/vibration, ataxia, dementia<15% (B12 def)B12 is needed for myelin; subacute combined degeneration of dorsal columns & corticospinal tracts — can precede anemia
Jaundice / scleral icterus, dark urine<15% (hemolysis)Unconjugated bilirubin from red-cell breakdown; hemoglobinuria in intravascular hemolysis
Koilonychia — concave "spoon" nails of chronic iron deficiency.
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Koilonychia iron deficiency anemia.jpg · CHeitz · CC BY 2.0
Ask about diet (vegan → B12), menstrual/GI blood loss, NSAID/aspirin/anticoagulant use, alcohol, and prior GI surgery up front — the history usually names the mechanism before the labs confirm it.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The stepwise lab cascade

CBC + indices + RDWFirst test. Confirms anemia, gives MCV (size) and RDW (variation — high in IDA, normal in thalassemia). Check WBC/platelets — bicytopenia/pancytopenia flags marrow disease.Initial
Reticulocyte count / RPIOrder with the CBC. Splits under-production (RPI <2) from blood loss/hemolysis (RPI ≥2). Drives the entire algorithm.Initial
Peripheral smearAny unexplained or multi-lineage cytopenia, suspected hemolysis, or abnormal indices. Morphology often names the diagnosis.Initial
Iron studies (ferritin, iron, TIBC, TSat)Microcytic or normocytic anemia. Fasting morning sample. Ferritin <30 = iron deficiency; interpret against inflammation.Microcytic/normo
B12 + folateMacrocytic anemia or neuro symptoms. If B12 200–300 (borderline) → add MMA + homocysteine.Macrocytic
Hemolysis panel — LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bili, DATRPI ≥2 without bleeding, or jaundice/dark urine. DAT splits immune vs non-immune.If retic high
Creatinine/eGFR, TSH, CRPNormocytic hypoproliferative anemia — screen for CKD (↓EPO), thyroid, and inflammation.Normocytic
Hemoglobin electrophoresisMicrocytosis with normal iron studies, or suspected thalassemia/sickle. Confirms hemoglobinopathy.Targeted
Bidirectional endoscopy (EGD + colonoscopy)All men and postmenopausal women with iron-deficiency anemia, and premenopausal women with alarm features — to exclude a GI source, especially malignancy (AGA 2020).IDA source
Iron-deficiency anemia is a diagnosis of a cause, not an endpoint. In an adult without an obvious source (menstruation, pregnancy, blood donation), assume occult GI blood loss and scope. Also send tissue transglutaminase (celiac) in unexplained IDA — malabsorption is a common miss.

Repletion — first-line → escalation

💊

Match the therapy to the broken step

1
Iron deficiency → treat the cause + ORAL iron
Correct the bleeding/malabsorption source, then replete stores.
▾
Oral iron refills the heme raw material so the marrow can build hemoglobin. Absorption is gated by hepcidin — which a large dose itself raises for ~24 h, so lower, spaced dosing absorbs a higher fraction.
Oral iron saltElemental Fe / tabStart → target (dose ladder)Why / notesIf intolerant
Ferrous sulfate 325 mg65 mgStart 1 tab every other day → if tolerated and losses are ongoing, up to 1 tab daily. Target ~40–60 mg elemental once daily or QOD; continue 3 months after Hgb normalizes to refill stores.Default first-line — cheapest. Alternate-day single AM dosing maximizes fractional absorption & halves GI side-effects (Stoffel 2017/2020)Switch salt, lower dose, or take with food (trades some absorption for tolerability) → then IV iron
Ferrous gluconate 324 mg38 mgStart 1 tab QOD–daily; titrate to ~40 mg elemental/dayLower elemental dose = often better toleratedFerrous fumarate or IV iron
Ferrous fumarate 325 mg106 mgStart ½–1 tab QOD; do not stack daily unless neededHighest elemental content per tabBisglycinate / polysaccharide iron complex (gentler)

How to take it: empty stomach with vitamin C (or orange juice) boosts absorption; separate from PPIs, calcium, coffee/tea, and levothyroxine by ≥2 h. Expected response: reticulocytosis by day 5–10; Hgb rises ~1–2 g/dL every 3–4 weeks. No response at 4 weeks → wrong diagnosis, ongoing loss, non-adherence, or malabsorption → reassess and consider IV.

If the prior dose is unknown (e.g., patient "was on iron"): restart ferrous sulfate 325 mg QOD and recheck CBC + reticulocytes + ferritin in 2–4 weeks rather than assuming failure.

2
IV iron — when oral won't work
Intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing loss, CKD, IBD, or need for rapid repletion.
▾
IV iron bypasses the gut and hepcidin, delivering iron straight to transferrin and stores — the answer whenever absorption is the problem (inflammation, IBD, bariatric surgery, CKD) or when you need to replete fast (2nd/3rd-trimester pregnancy, pre-op, symptomatic).
IV ironDose per session → totalRegimenNotes / monitoring
Ferric derisomaltose (Monoferric)1000 mgSingle dose (if ≥50 kg) over ≥20 minOne-and-done total-dose infusion; low hypophosphatemia risk
Ferric carboxymaltose (Injectafer)750 mg × 2 (or 15 mg/kg)Two doses ≥7 days apartWatch for hypophosphatemia (check phosphate if repeated/symptomatic)
Iron sucrose (Venofer)200 mg × up to 5Multiple sessionsLong safety record incl. pregnancy & dialysis
Ferumoxytol (Feraheme)510 mg × 2Two doses 3–8 days apartCan interfere with MRI for weeks
LMW iron dextran (INFeD)Total-dose infusionSingle large infusion after test doseTest dose first; highest anaphylaxis risk of the group
Total iron deficit (Ganzoni): deficit (mg) = weight (kg) × (target Hgb − actual Hgb, g/dL) × 2.4 + iron stores (≈500 mg for adults ≥35 kg). Most adults need ~1000–1500 mg total. Modern practice favors simple fixed-dose regimens (e.g., 1000 mg derisomaltose) over Ganzoni arithmetic.
3
Cause-specific — B12/folate, ESA, referral, transfusion
Fix the specific missing lever.
▾
Deficiency / driverStartTitration → maintenanceWhy / notes
Vitamin B12 (severe / neuro / malabsorption)1000 mcg IM daily × 1 week→ weekly × 4 weeks → monthly for life (or 1000–2000 mcg PO daily if absorption intact & mild)Restores DNA synthesis & myelin. IM guarantees delivery in pernicious anemia/post-gastrectomy

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How common comorbidities change the anemia & its management

ComorbidityEffect on the anemiaManagement change
CKD↓EPO + ↑hepcidin → hypoproliferative normocytic anemiaReplete iron to ferritin >100/TSat >20%, then ESA to Hgb 10–11.5 (not >13); IV iron preferred on dialysis (PIVOTAL)
Heart failureIron deficiency (often functional) worsens symptoms & hospitalizations even without anemiaIV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) if ferritin <100, or 100–299 with TSat <20% (AFFIRM-AHF, IRONMAN) — improves function/QoL
IBD (Crohn/UC)Blood loss + inflammation (hepcidin) → mixed IDA/ACD; oral iron poorly absorbed & may worsen gut symptomsIV iron first-line in active disease
Inflammation / malignancy / infectionHigh hepcidin traps iron; ferritin falsely reassuringTreat the driver; use ferritin <100 (or <300 + TSat<20%) cutoff; consider sTfR
PregnancyPhysiologic dilution + high fetal iron demand; IDA commonOral iron first; IV iron in 2nd/3rd trimester for intolerance or rapid need; folate 0.4–1 mg pre-conception
Post-bariatric / gastrectomy / atrophic gastritisImpaired iron & B12 absorption (acid/intrinsic factor loss)Long-term IV iron + parenteral/high-dose B12
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: PPIs & H2-blockers blunt oral iron absorption (separate dosing or switch to IV); NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants drive occult GI loss — review the indication in any IDA; calcium, levothyroxine, coffee/tea, fluoroquinolones/tetracyclines chelate oral iron (separate by ≥2 h); do not start an ESA while iron-deficient or above target Hgb (thrombosis risk); avoid oxidant drugs (dapsone, sulfa, nitrofurantoin, primaquine) in G6PD deficiency.

Screening for this population

GradeRecommendationPopulation
I*Screening for iron-deficiency anemia (asymptomatic pregnant) — current statement is an I (insufficient evidence); many obstetric bodies still screen with CBCAsymptomatic pregnant persons

*The USPSTF currently issues I statements (insufficient evidence) rather than Grade A/B for routine IDA screening/supplementation in asymptomatic pregnancy — stated honestly here rather than assigning an unearned grade. Prevention leverage in anemia is mostly through screening for and treating the underlying cause (GI malignancy, menorrhagia, celiac).

Escalate

When to refer / send to ED

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission / specialist

Send to the ED for: Hgb <7 with symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea at rest, syncope, tachycardia/hypotension), active or brisk bleeding, hemodynamic instability, or new schistocytes + thrombocytopenia (possible TTP — emergency).
Refer to hematology for: unexplained hemolysis, pancytopenia or suspected MDS/aplasia, suspected hemoglobinopathy, or anemia not responding to appropriate repletion. Refer to GI for endoscopic evaluation of any iron-deficiency anemia without an obvious non-GI source.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Admit for the consequences of anemia (instability, ischemia) or the cause (active bleeding, hemolytic crisis), not the number alone.

  • Hemodynamic instability / active or brisk bleeding — melena, hematemesis, hematochezia, trauma, obvious source with tachycardia/hypotension.
  • Symptomatic anemia — angina, decompensated heart failure, syncope, dyspnea at rest, altered mentation, or ECG ischemia.
  • Severe anemia — Hgb <7 g/dL (or <8 with cardiovascular disease) needing transfusion, especially if acute.
  • Hematologic emergency — suspected TTP (schistocytes + thrombocytopenia), severe hemolytic crisis, aplastic/pancytopenic crisis, or febrile neutropenia with anemia.
  • Anemia + comorbid decompensation — anemia unmasking ACS, or where rapid workup/transfusion cannot be done outpatient.

Treat

Acute management & transfusion

💊

Stabilize → transfuse to threshold → treat the cause

1
Resuscitate & transfuse to a restrictive threshold
Restrictive ≥ liberal in almost every trial.
▾
Transfusion is instant "fleet replacement." But over-transfusion causes harm (volume overload, alloimmunization, cost, and — in trials — no benefit or worse outcomes). A restrictive threshold is at least as safe as liberal (TRICC, TRISS, FOCUS, REALITY) — so transfuse for a threshold + symptoms, not to "normalize."
Scenario (AABB 2023)Transfuse if Hgb <
Most hospitalized adults, hemodynamically stable (incl. critically ill) — the only strongly graded 2023 recommendation7 g/dL
Cardiac surgery7.5 g/dL (non-graded remark)
Orthopedic surgery or pre-existing cardiovascular disease8 g/dL (2016 strong rec; 2023 remark)
Acute coronary syndrome / acute MIUncertain — a liberal strategy (~10 g/dL) may be reasonable (MINT 2023); individualize
Active major hemorrhage / hemodynamic instabilityResuscitate to perfusion, not a number — activate MTP (see ICU)

Transfuse one unit at a time and reassess; recheck Hgb after each (or after equilibration if not bleeding). Each unit of pRBCs raises Hgb by ~1 g/dL (Hct ~3%) in a 70–80 kg adult who isn't bleeding.

2
Replete the deficiency — IV iron, B12/folate
Faster inpatient correction; reduces future transfusion.
▾

IV iron is ideal inpatient for iron-deficiency anemia (rapid, bypasses gut/hepcidin) — e.g., ferric derisomaltose 1000 mg once or ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg. It reduces the number of units transfused and is preferred over oral in inflammation, IBD, CKD, and post-op. Give B12 1000 mcg IM and/or folate if deficient — watch for hypokalemia as brisk erythropoiesis consumes potassium.

Draw iron studies/B12/folate before transfusing when feasible — transfused blood confounds these for weeks.
3
Source control & disease-specific therapy
Stop the loss; treat the mechanism.
▾

Bleeding: endoscopy (GI bleed), IR embolization, or surgery; reverse anticoagulation (see ICU reversal table); PPI infusion for upper GI bleed; TXA for hyperfibrinolytic bleeding. Hemolysis: corticosteroids for warm AIHA, keep the patient warm + treat cause for cold agglutinin; TTP → urgent plasma exchange + steroids (do not transfuse platelets). Aplasia/MDS/malignancy: hematology, transfusion support ± growth factors.

Monitor

What to trend each day

📈

Daily targets

  • Serial Hgb/Hct — trend (q6–8h while bleeding, daily once stable). A falling Hgb after resuscitation = ongoing loss until proven otherwise; remember Hgb lags acute hemorrhage until hemodilution.
  • Reticulocyte response — confirms marrow is recovering after repletion/bleeding control.
  • Hemodynamics & symptoms — HR, BP, orthostatics, chest pain, urine output, mentation.
  • Signs of ongoing loss — stool color, drain/NG output, abdominal exam.
  • Transfusion tolerance — volume status/TACO in HF/CKD/elderly (consider furosemide between units); post-transfusion Hgb increment (a poor increment suggests ongoing loss or hemolysis).
  • Electrolytes — K⁺, Ca²⁺ (citrate binds calcium with large-volume transfusion), Mg²⁺.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for: ongoing hemorrhage despite resuscitation or need for massive transfusion (≥4 units/hr or ≥10 units/24h, or MTP activation); shock (SBP <90/MAP <65, lactate rising) or pressor requirement; Hgb continuing to fall despite adequate transfusion; airway compromise (massive hematemesis); suspected TTP needing plasma exchange; or any anemia with end-organ ischemia (ACS, altered mental status) requiring intensive monitoring.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: no active bleeding & a stable Hgb on ≥2 checks (typically ≥24 h off transfusion), hemodynamically stable, the cause identified with a follow-up plan (e.g., outpatient endoscopy booked, iron/B12 repletion prescribed, hematology follow-up), and safe symptom burden.

Home

Stable Hgb, cause addressed, can complete oral/IV iron & follow-up as outpatient.

Home health

Needs infusion visits (IV iron), wound/ostomy care, or monitoring but otherwise independent.

SNF

Deconditioned/frail, needs 24h skilled nursing & <3h therapy/day before going home.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Functional decline (e.g., post-hemorrhage) able to tolerate ≥3h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex needs (e.g., ongoing transfusion support with other organ support).

Hospice / palliative

Transfusion-dependent anemia from advanced malignancy/MDS with comfort-focused goals.
🫀 ICU — hemorrhagic shock & massive transfusion
Admit

ICU triggers & shock staging

🚨

Hemorrhagic shock classes (ATLS)

In acute blood loss the anemia is often the last thing to change — Hgb is initially normal until fluid shifts in. Read the physiology, not the number.

ClassBlood lossHRBP / pulse pressureMentation & UOP
I<15% (<750 mL)<100NormalNormal; UOP >30 mL/h
II15–30% (750–1500 mL)100–120Normal SBP, narrow pulse pressureMildly anxious; UOP 20–30
III30–40% (1500–2000 mL)120–140↓ SBPAnxious/confused; UOP 5–15
IV>40% (>2000 mL)>140↓↓ SBPLethargic; UOP negligible
Class III–IV, ongoing hemorrhage needing massive transfusion, shock/pressors, lactate rising, or a hematologic emergency (TTP, severe hemolysis) belongs in the unit. Young patients compensate then crash — tachycardia + narrow pulse pressure is the early warning.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Access: two large-bore peripheral IVs (≥16–18 g) > a triple-lumen for speed; consider a large introducer (Cordis) or rapid transfuser for massive hemorrhage; arterial line for continuous BP + frequent labs.
  • Trend: Hgb/Hct, platelets, PT/INR/aPTT, fibrinogen, lactate, ionized calcium, K⁺, ABG. Point-of-care Hgb and viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) guide component therapy where available.
  • Targets in hemorrhage: perfusion (MAP, lactate clearance, urine output) over a Hgb number; fibrinogen >150–200 mg/dL, platelets >50k (>100k if CNS bleed), ionized Ca²⁺ >1.1 mmol/L, temperature & pH near-normal (avoid the "lethal triad" of hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy).
Resuscitate

Massive transfusion protocol

💉

Balanced 1:1:1 resuscitation

In major hemorrhage you lose whole blood — replacing only red cells dilutes clotting factors and platelets and worsens bleeding. Balanced resuscitation (plasma:platelets:RBC ≈ 1:1:1) reconstitutes something close to whole blood. In PROPPR (2015), 1:1:1 achieved hemostasis more often and reduced death from exsanguination at 24 h vs 1:1:2, with no increase in complications.
Component / adjunctDosePurpose / target
pRBC : FFP : platelets1 : 1 : 1 (e.g., 6:6:1 pooled)Balanced resuscitation; O-neg / type-specific until crossmatched
Tranexamic acid (trauma)1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h, within 3 h of injuryAntifibrinolytic; reduces death from bleeding in trauma (CRASH-2). Not beneficial in GI bleed (HALT-IT) — don't use routinely there
Calcium (chloride/gluconate)1 g CaCl₂ (or 2–3 g gluconate) per few units; titrateCitrate in stored blood chelates calcium → ionized hypocalcemia impairs clotting & contractility; keep iCa >1.1
Fibrinogen (cryo / concentrate)10 units cryo or per assayKeep fibrinogen >150–200 mg/dL
Activate the MTP early (e.g., ≥4 units in 1 h with ongoing bleeding, or predicted need). Warm all fluids/products, and watch for hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, and dilutional coagulopathy as you go.
Reverse

Reversal of anticoagulation

🧯

Anticoagulant-associated bleeding

Agent bleeding onReversalDoseNotes
Warfarin (VKA)4-factor PCC + vitamin K4F-PCC 25–50 U/kg (INR-based) + vitamin K 10 mg IVPCC replaces II, VII, IX, X faster than FFP; vitamin K sustains reversal
Dabigatran (direct thrombin)Idarucizumab5 g IV (2 × 2.5 g)Specific monoclonal antidote; dialyzable as backup
Apixaban / rivaroxaban (factor Xa)Andexanet alfa, or 4F-PCCAndexanet per dose/timing protocol; else 4F-PCC 50 U/kgAndexanet costly/limited; PCC is the common practical option
Heparin (UFH)Protamine1 mg per 100 U heparin in last 2–3 h (max 50 mg)Partial reversal only for LMWH
Antiplatelet-associatedPlatelets ± desmopressinPlatelets if life-threatening/CNS bleed; DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kgPlatelet transfusion benefit is uncertain outside neurosurgical bleeding
Alongside reversal: hold the offending drug, achieve source control (endoscopy/IR/surgery), and resuscitate. Balance rebound thrombosis risk (mechanical valve, recent VTE/PE) when reversing.
Rescue

Advanced / refractory options

⚙️

When standard measures fail

  • Refractory hemorrhage: damage-control surgery, angioembolization (IR), endoscopic hemostasis, REBOA in selected trauma; intraoperative cell salvage (autotransfusion) to reduce allogeneic exposure.
  • TTP: urgent therapeutic plasma exchange + high-dose steroids ± caplacizumab; avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding (can fuel microthrombi).
  • Severe autoimmune hemolysis: steroids, transfuse the "least incompatible" units for life-threatening anemia (don't withhold), IVIG/rituximab per hematology.
  • Jehovah's Witness / bloodless: maximize erythropoiesis (IV iron + high-dose ESA + B12/folate), minimize phlebotomy, tolerate lower Hgb, use TXA/cell salvage.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: bleeding is controlled (source addressed), Hgb stable without transfusion for ≥24 h, off vasopressors with normalized lactate & adequate urine output, coagulopathy/electrolytes corrected, and no further MTP activation. Not yet if: Hgb still drifting down, recurrent melena/hematemesis, escalating transfusion requirement, or unresolved TTP/hemolysis. ICU disposition otherwise mirrors the wards (home → LTAC → hospice) once stable.
Shared

Clinical pearls & a bedside discriminator

💡

High-yield pearls

  1. Reticulocytes before everything. RPI <2 = the marrow isn't responding (production problem); RPI ≥2 = it is (blood loss or hemolysis). This one number sorts half the differential.
  2. Ferritin <30 ng/mL is essentially diagnostic of iron deficiency (AGA 2020 uses a more sensitive <45 in anemic patients) — but because ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, use <100 (or <300 + TSat <20%) in CKD, HF, IBD, or active inflammation.
  3. Give iron every other day. A single large dose raises hepcidin for ~24 h and blocks the next dose — alternate-day, single morning dosing absorbs a higher fraction with fewer GI side-effects (Stoffel).
  4. RDW splits microcytosis: high RDW + low MCV → iron deficiency; normal RDW + low MCV + high RBC count → thalassemia trait.
  5. Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC): <13 → thalassemia trait, >13 → iron deficiency — a fast bedside filter (calculator below).
  6. Check B12 before giving folate. Folate alone corrects megaloblastic anemia but lets B12 neuropathy (subacute combined degeneration) progress irreversibly.
  7. Borderline B12 (200–300 pg/mL)? Send MMA + homocysteine. Elevated MMA confirms true B12 deficiency when the level is equivocal.
  8. Oral iron failing in an inflamed patient is expected, not a mystery — hepcidin blocks gut absorption. Go IV (also first-line in IBD, CKD, and when you need speed).
  9. Don't transfuse to a number. Restrictive (Hgb 7; 8 with cardiovascular disease) is as safe as liberal — one unit at a time, then reassess (AABB 2023).
  10. Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = TTP until excluded — start plasma exchange emergently; do not transfuse platelets.
  11. Hgb lags acute hemorrhage. A "normal" Hgb right after a big bleed is falsely reassuring until hemodilution catches up — treat the physiology.
  12. IV iron helps heart failure even without anemia if ferritin <100 (or <300 + TSat <20%) — AFFIRM-AHF/IRONMAN improved function and reduced HF hospitalizations (both narrowly missed their primary endpoint, but guidelines endorse it).
  13. Continue oral iron 3 months after the Hgb normalizes to refill stores — stopping at a normal Hgb guarantees relapse.
  14. A poor post-transfusion Hgb increment (<1 g/dL/unit without dilution) means ongoing loss or hemolysis — go looking.

🧮 Mentzer index — microcytic anemia discriminator

Enter MCV and RBC count.

A screening heuristic only — confirm with iron studies and hemoglobin electrophoresis. Not valid in mixed deficiencies.
